Oil Prices Tumble Again
 
Plus, AI jitters at banks and Berkshire’s home-builder bet
 
By Heard on the Street Staff
 
 
STRINGER/REUTERS
 

This is an edition of the Markets P.M. newsletter, a recap of the day’s most important markets moves, delivered after the closing bell. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

What Happened in Markets Today

 

Stocks lost momentum as potential threats took center stage. Disruption from AI and geopolitical tensions flattened the market after Monday’s sharp tech-fueled rally. The S&P 500 was little changed, while the Nasdaq Composite index rose 0.5% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 185 points, or 0.4%.

 

Oil prices withstood President Trump’s tough talk. Speaking at the United Nations, Trump described one of his options as moving to “annihilate” Iran, though he also said he was open to peace. Still, Brent crude futures ended the day lower for the fifth time in a row, falling about 1% to close the session below $100 a barrel, at $99.25. A report said that Iran has proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz, were the U.S. to lift its blockade.

 

AI’s latest offering sent financial stocks tumbling. Shares of banks and brokerages were lower on Tuesday, as investors considered the risk that agents like Meta’s Muse will automate decisions about money. Charles Schwab was down more than 6% in the move.

 

Chip and memory stocks rallied. The PHLX Semiconductor index was up 2%, extending its streak of gains to six sessions in a row. Monolithic Power Systems led the market with an 8% rise. Sandisk was up almost 7% and Seagate Technology and Micron Technology were up around 5%.

 

Lennar shares jumped on Berkshire’s buying. Shares of the home builder surged more than 6%. Berkshire Hathaway revealed that it had added to its ownership of the company, and now holds around a 10% stake.

One Big Story

 
 
SPENCER PLATT/GETTY IMAGES
 

A batch of 2021-era apartment loans is in trouble. Last week’s Federal Reserve rate increase might force owners and their lenders to sell underperforming properties and finally give bargain hunters a chance to buy real estate at low prices.

 

Pickings have been slim for investors looking to buy distressed property at cheap prices in recent years. Lenders extended or modified loans to avoid taking a loss in a distressed sale. Only owners of troubled office buildings were willing to take a hit. But recently, troubled assets have started to hit the market.
